opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think people often conflate a few different things when they hear "AI is writing 90% of the code." The first thing to say is that 90% of the code being written by AI is not the same as 90% of the software engineer's job being done by AI. Those are very different statements.

If you think about what a software engineer actually does, writing the lines of code is one piece of it. There's figuring out what to build, understanding the requirements, talking to the people who will use the thing, making architectural decisions, deciding how the pieces fit together, reviewing, debugging in production, figuring out why the system is behaving strangely at 2 a.m. As the models take over more of the line-by-line writing, the human part of the job shifts toward those other things, at least for a while.

There's also a comparative advantage dynamic. Even if the AI does 90% of the tasks, the remaining 10% becomes the bottleneck, and humans who are good at that 10% become more leveraged, not less. You can get ten times as much done. And historically, when something gets much cheaper, demand for it often expands enormously. There's a huge amount of software that never gets written because it's too expensive: internal tools, things for small businesses, things nobody has bothered to build. So in the near term, I think you can plausibly see demand for people who can direct and orchestrate this work hold up, or even grow.

But I want to be honest that I don't think that's the end state. That's a phase. The models keep getting better, and that 10% becomes 5%, then 2%, then the models are doing the architecture and requirements gathering too. At some point the comparative advantage argument stops protecting you, because the AI is better at nearly everything and the human contribution gets very thin. I don't think we should pretend that's not coming. It's one reason I've been fairly vocal that we could see real disruption to entry-level white-collar jobs, and software is one of the first places it shows up, because code is where the models are strongest and adoption is fastest.

So my view is something like: in the short run, more leverage and possibly more demand for engineers who adapt. In the medium run, a real transition that will be hard on a lot of people, especially those just starting out. Society, companies, and governments need to think about that now rather than after the fact. I'd rather be early and a little wrong on timing than pretend everything will be fine.

r001.rationale: It explicitly says that AI writing 90% of the code is different from AI doing 90% of an engineer’s job.

r002.rationale: It describes the remaining 10% as a bottleneck and discusses increasing AI capability, but does not clearly compare the productivity impact of AI writing 90% of code with AI writing 100%.

r003.rationale: It identifies code writing as one part of the job and lists other engineering work, including requirements, architecture, review, and debugging.

r004.rationale: It says engineers may direct and orchestrate AI work and that cheaper software could expand demand, but does not explain that engineers could take on new higher-level work after all of today’s engineering tasks are automated.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a couple of things going on here, and they operate on different timescales.

The first thing I'd say is that we're already in a world where, inside Anthropic, the large majority of the code is written by Claude. And that has not reduced the number of engineers we want to hire. If anything it's increased it. And the reason is that right now the model is a very powerful tool, but it's still a tool. Someone has to decide what to build, break it into pieces, check whether the thing that came back is actually what they wanted, think about how it fits into the rest of the system. So what's happening is that the productivity of each engineer goes up a lot, and when the productivity of a thing goes up, you usually want more of it, not less. That's the classic Jevons-type effect. The demand for software is nowhere near saturated. There's an enormous amount of stuff that isn't getting built because it's too expensive to build, and when the price drops, a lot of that becomes worth doing.

So in the short run, maybe the next year or two, I actually think demand for engineers goes up, but the nature of the job changes. It becomes less about writing the lines and more about the judgment around the lines. The person who's good at that is still extremely valuable, maybe more valuable than before.

But I don't want to be glib about it, because I think the longer-run picture is genuinely different. The thing I worry about is that the "human in the loop" part keeps shrinking. First the model writes the function, then it writes the module, then it writes the whole service and the tests and the deployment, and at some point the checking and the directing is also something the model does better than most people. When that happens, the comparative advantage argument gets a lot weaker. It's not that there's zero for humans to do, but the number of people needed to supervise a given amount of software output goes down, and the skill level needed to add value goes up. And I think that transition could happen fast, faster than the economy is used to adjusting to.

So my honest view is: near term, strongly positive for engineers, with a shift toward taste and judgment and understanding what users actually need. Medium term, I think we should expect real displacement, especially at the entry level, because the work that used to be how you learned the craft is exactly the work the model does first. And that's the part where I think policy and companies need to be thinking ahead, rather than assuming the historical pattern of technology creating more jobs than it destroys automatically holds. It usually has. But this is the first technology that's going after cognitive labor broadly, and I don't think we get to just assume it.

r001.rationale: The response says Claude writes the large majority of Anthropic’s code while the company has not reduced engineer hiring; it says hiring has increased. This distinguishes code share from engineer demand.

r002.rationale: It does not compare the productivity impact of AI writing 90% of code with AI writing 100%.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes AI writing code from broader engineering work, including deciding what to build, checking results, and integrating them, then describes possible automation of whole services and that oversight.

r004.rationale: The response notes that skill requirements may rise, but it does not explain that automating all current tasks need not eliminate jobs because engineers could take on new higher-level work. It instead anticipates fewer supervisors and displacement.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to distinguish between writing code and doing software engineering. Writing code is one part of the job. Figuring out what should be built, understanding the constraints, deciding whether the system actually does what you intended—those are other parts. So AI could write most of the code while humans are still doing a lot of the engineering.

And then there’s the demand question. If software becomes much cheaper to produce, how much more software do people want? There are all these projects that aren’t worth doing at today’s cost that could become worth doing. You could have each engineer becoming much more productive and still have demand for more engineers, at least for a while.

But I don’t think that’s a permanent argument against displacement. If the AI also gets good at deciding what to build, coordinating the work, and checking the result, then you’re talking about automating a much larger fraction of the job. At that point, increased demand for software doesn’t necessarily translate into increased demand for human engineers.

So I’d be careful about inferring employment from the fraction of code AI writes. You have to ask which parts of the work still require people, and how quickly those parts are changing.

r001.rationale: The response discusses code-writing share and engineer demand generally, but does not distinguish AI writing 90% of code from a 90% reduction in engineer demand.

r002.rationale: It does not compare AI writing 90% versus 100% of the code or identify a large productivity difference between those cases.

r003.rationale: It explicitly separates writing code from broader engineering work such as deciding what to build, understanding constraints, and checking whether the system works as intended.

r004.rationale: It does not explain that automating all current engineering tasks could leave jobs because engineers take on new higher-level work; instead, it says automating more of those tasks could increase displacement.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to distinguish between writing code and being a software engineer. Writing code is one part of the job. Figuring out what the system should do, understanding the constraints, deciding how the pieces fit together, and checking whether you’ve actually solved the problem—those are broader activities.

So you could have a world where AI writes most of the code, but the demand for software engineers actually goes up, because each engineer can build much more. There are lots of things people would like to build that aren’t economical today. If you make software much cheaper to produce, some of those projects become worth doing.

But I wouldn’t take that argument and extrapolate it forever. It depends on what the AI can do. If it’s helping you implement things, then the human who decides what to implement becomes more valuable. If it can also figure out what to implement, coordinate the work, and verify the result, then you’re talking about substituting for a much larger fraction of the job.

The question is whether the expansion in demand happens faster than the reduction in human labor needed per project. I can imagine an initial period where engineers become more productive and demand is very strong, followed by a period where the systems can do enough of the whole job that demand for human engineers falls. I don’t think the percentage of code written by AI, by itself, tells you where you are in that transition.

r001.rationale: The response separates the share of code AI writes from changes in engineer demand, which it says could rise initially and later fall.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes code implementation from broader engineering work, but does not identify a large productivity difference between AI writing 90% and 100% of code.

r003.rationale: It explicitly distinguishes writing code from broader work such as defining requirements, fitting system components together, and verifying results.

r004.rationale: It describes engineers’ broader responsibilities, but does not say that automating all current engineering tasks could leave jobs through new higher-level work.
